Before you start

Students learn why losing a friend hurts like an injury, how common it is in the teen years, and how to weigh repair, reset, or release. Bring index cards, use only the slide scenarios since former friends may be sitting in the same circle, and never suggest anyone owes a second chance.

Every student in the room

Friendship breakups ripple through shared teams, neighborhoods and faith communities, and for an autistic student or a student who just moved, one ending can take out most of their social world.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why a friendship ending hurts like an injury and why endings are so common in the teen years, name a feeling specifically, and weigh repair, reset, or release. Nobody shares a real friendship.

Materials

  • Scrap paper for the opening guess
  • Index cards for the private reflection
  • The student page link (last slide) to share after advisory

Flow

  1. 6 minThe guess and the real number (anonymous)
  2. 5 minWhy it hurts, and what helps
  3. 4 minRepair, reset, or release? (pairs)
  4. 3 minOne specific word (private)
  5. 2 minWaves, and the student page

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

The guess and the real number (3), why it hurts (2), repair, reset, or release with one scenario (3), waves and the student page (2).

Before you teach
Former friends may be in the same circle.

Advisory groups are small, and two people who used to be close may sit across from each other. Use only the slide scenarios. Don't ask for stories, names, or what happened.

Don't push repair.

Some friendships should end. Present repair, reset and release as equal choices, and never suggest a student owes anyone a second chance.

Unsafe friendships go to an adult.

If a student says a friendship was controlling or threatening, or that an old group is targeting them online or in person, thank them, move on, and follow up privately that day with a counselor or dean.

Sadness that lasts goes to a counselor.

The student page names sadness most days for more than two weeks, and big changes in sleep, eating or grades. Don't ask about these in the circle. Any disclosure goes to a counselor the same day.

Leave room for the one who ended it.

Students who stepped away may feel guilty or get cast as the bad guy. Lena's card gives them a way in: you can know it was right and still miss someone.

Keep the brain science light.

The point is that the hurt is real. Some of the brain findings are debated, so say "researchers found" and skip the anatomy if time is short.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

It ripples through shared communities.

Two friends may share a religious community, a neighborhood, a team, or families who know each other. An ending can change where a student feels comfortable going, including a place of worship. Name that as part of the loss.

Who students can tell.

"Tell one person the real version" can mean a sibling, a cousin, a grandparent, a coach, or a parent or caregiver. Not every student can bring this home, so always name a counselor too.

Identity and friendships.

Some friendships end around coming out, or around how a friend reacted to someone's identity. Don't ask why any friendship ended. If a student was outed or is being targeted for who they are, that's a counselor conversation that day.

Friendship looks different for different brains.

Autistic students and students with social anxiety may have fewer close friends, so one ending can take out most of their social world. The run-in plan gives a script. Don't measure a good friend by how social someone is.

Anyone can grieve a friendship.

Students may hear that only girls have friendship drama. Say plainly that losing a close friend hurts anyone, and mix genders in your examples, as Maya and Jordan do.

Moving and distance.

Students who moved schools, cities or countries may have lost friendships to distance, and may be grieving friends who speak another language. Drift counts, and staying in touch across time zones is a real form of repair.

What the research says

People left out of a simple online ball-toss game showed more activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate, a region that also responds to how upsetting physical pain feels. The more it rose, the more upset they said they were.

Eisenberger, Lieberman and Williams, Science, 2003

In the same study, people with more activity in the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex reported less distress. It seems to act as a brake, and it's still maturing through the teens.

Eisenberger, Lieberman and Williams, 2003

When people who had been through an unwanted breakup looked at a photo of their ex, areas that process physical pain became active. Other scientists argue these areas respond to anything intense, so the overlap is debated.

Kross et al., Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2011

Putting a feeling into words reduced the amygdala's response and raised activity in the brake region.

Lieberman et al., Psychological Science, 2007

Researchers followed 410 students from seventh grade through twelfth. Fewer than 1 in 4 seventh-grade friendships lasted to the next school year, and about 1 in 100 made it to senior year.

Hartl, Laursen and Cillessen, Psychological Science, 2015

Friendships most often ended when the two people grew different, in grades, popularity, aggression, or gender.

Hartl, Laursen and Cillessen, 2015

Writing about a painful experience for a few short sessions is linked with better health and mood afterward. The effects are modest, and they hold up across many studies.

Pennebaker, Psychological Science, 1997
